title: Kiss the joy as it flies
word: Kiss the joy as it flies

segments.voice: That was the week of Wordsworth and Blake. Getting and spending. Trailing clouds of glory. Spots of time. Who made the tyger. Little lamb. And yesterday, the divine image: mercy, pity, peace, love, wearing a human face. Now, the last of Blake.
screen: `MERCY, PITY, PEACE, LOVE.` → `THE LAST OF BLAKE.`

segments.voice: Ever held a perfect moment so tightly, filming it, replaying it, planning the next one, that you half missed it? Blake has four lines on that, written in his private notebook under the title Eternity: "He who binds to himself a joy / Does the winged life destroy; / But he who kisses the joy as it flies / Lives in eternity's sun rise." So how do you hold a joy without crushing it? You don't grab it. You kiss it as it flies.
screen: `HELD SO TIGHT YOU MISSED IT.` → `A PRIVATE NOTEBOOK.` → `ETERNITY.` → `KISS IT AS IT FLIES.`

segments.voice: Notice the two verbs. Binds is what you do to a captive. Kisses is what you do to someone you love, at the door, before you let them go. Now look at where eternity sits in those lines. Not later, not after death, but in a sunrise you live in now, the moment you stop binding. That's Blake's teaching: eternity breaks into time when you love a thing without trapping it. Some readers hear an older story underneath. In Exodus, God feeds Israel in the wilderness with manna, fresh each morning, enough for the day. Some tried to keep it overnight, and it "bred worms, and stank." A gift for today goes bad when it's hoarded. It's the same day-sized gift Jesus teaches his followers to ask for: "Give us this day our daily bread." And the stories of Blake's own last days, gathered by his biographer Alexander Gilchrist, say he lived his line. Ill and near the end, he kept drawing, sketched his wife Catherine and told her she had been an angel to him, and died singing. He didn't bind the joy. He sang it as it flew.
screen: `ETERNITY'S SUNRISE: NOW.` · `MANNA: ENOUGH FOR THE DAY.` · `GIVE US THIS DAY.` · `BLAKE DIED SINGING.` · then, large: `KISS IT AS IT FLIES.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, listen to one sound you can't keep: a bird, rain, traffic, someone laughing in another room. Let each bit of it arrive and go without trying to hold on. If something lovely passes through, notice it, thank it, and let it fly.
Kiss the joy as it flies: Blake's picture, in his notebook poem Eternity, of loving a joy without trapping it. Bind it, and the winged life dies.
